name: Detoxification foot pads

lead: Detox foot pads are sticky pads, usually containing bamboo or wood vinegar and sometimes tourmaline and herbs, that are stuck to the soles at bedtime and peeled off in the morning. Sellers presented them as pulling toxins out of the body, with promised benefits including more energy, weight loss and a fresher, healthier look.

The pads turn from light to dark during the night, which sellers presented as proof of detoxing. In 2008 National Public Radio reported that the pads turn grey when exposed to moisture such as sweat, and a lab test found no heavy metals in used pads. In 2009 the US Federal Trade Commission sued Kinoki's marketers, and a court ban followed in 2010.

paras: In practice, one pad goes on each sole when going to bed, is worn overnight and is removed in the morning, usually as a multi-night course. Users commonly judge results by the colour of the used pad, and some pair the pads with a general wellness routine.

The main documented issues are regulatory rather than medical: the FTC said the advertised claims were false or lacked support, and state and federal actions followed. Adhesive skin irritation is possible with any sticky pad, and the products are not an approved treatment for any condition.

angle.text: Sellers marketed foot pads as a way to feel and look healthier, with weight loss and less fatigue as headline claims. Users judge results by how dark the pad is after a night.

lead: Detoxification foot pads are adhesive pads placed on the soles of the feet overnight. Manufacturers claim they draw toxins from the body through the feet, and the pads usually look dark brown or grey by morning, which marketing presented as evidence of what had been removed [1][2]. For appearance, the promised payoffs were weight loss, less fatigue and a healthier look, which is why they were sold alongside beauty and slimming products [2].

Typical ingredients are bamboo vinegar or wood vinegar, tourmaline, herbs such as houttuynia and binders such as chitosan, with brands such as Kinoki selling them in the United States from about 2007 [3][1]. NPR testing in 2008 found that the pads turn from white to grey when they get wet, including from sweat, and that used pads contained no heavy metals [1].

The pads drew regulatory attention. The US FTC sued Kinoki's marketers in January 2009, alleging that claims of removing toxins and treating conditions from diabetes to weight problems were false or unsupported, and in November 2010 a court imposed a ban on the marketers [2][1].

paras: The pads are worn on the soles overnight and are marketed on the idea that the feet are an exit route for toxins, heavy metals and metabolic waste [3][1]. Product ads linked the pads to reflexology and to Japanese or Asian tradition [3].

The FTC's complaint quotes ads saying the pads could remove toxins, heavy metals, parasites and cellulite and were good for conditions including arthritis, diabetes, fatigue, insomnia and weight loss [2].

In August 2008, NPR reported that the pads turn from white to grey when moisture, including sweat, reaches them, so the colour change does not itself show that anything was absorbed from the body [1]. Ingredients such as wood vinegar are listed in Grokipedia's summary as the components involved in darkening [3].

In January 2008 the US FDA warned about risks from many imported products, including several foot patch brands, and in April 2008 it investigated Kinoki's claims [1]. The FTC filed suit against Xacta 3000, Inc. and two principals in January 2009, alleging that all advertising claims were false or lacked support when made [2]. A federal court imposed a ban on the marketers in November 2010 [1].

No studies found. Journalistic testing exists: NPR's 2008 laboratory test of used pads found no heavy metals [1]. Companies such as Japan's Kenrico cite their own research supporting health claims, which the Wikipedia article reports as lacking independent evidence [1].
Forum users on T Nation discussed Kinoki ads in 2008, with the pads' brown colour by morning the central point of debate [4].
